output.answer: Anthropic filed its S-1 with the SEC on Oct 26, 2026, for a Nasdaq listing under ticker "ANT," and per a Nov 10 amended filing will offer 825 million Class A shares at $70–$78, with pricing expected Nov 18 and trading Nov 19 — up to $64.35 billion in proceeds and a fully diluted valuation up to $1.405 trillion. The filing reveals explosive but costly growth: revenue of $33.24 billion for the nine months ended Sept 30, 2026 (up ~1,200% year over year, with a ~$81 billion run-rate at the end of October) against a $104 billion net loss driven mostly by fair-value changes on convertible notes and derivative liabilities, plus ~$895.4 billion in purchase commitments substantially all for compute and infrastructure. Governance is unusual: Anthropic is a public benefit corporation whose seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, hold 50.1% of voting power through a single Class F share — a structure the company says has "no direct public company precedent." The S-1 devotes more than 90 pages to risk factors, including that its AI safety safeguards "are incomplete" and may be circumvented, customer concentration (top five customers = 25% of business), a historically compute-constrained operation, and heavy exposure to datacenter regulation. Separately, AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC have agreed to buy $26 billion of Class N stock in a private placement at the IPO price.
caveats: The IPO had not priced or begun trading as of Nov 11, 2026: the registration statement has not yet become effective, and pricing (Nov 18) and trading (Nov 19) dates are per sources cited by CNBC, not a company announcement.
The final valuation is uncertain: analyst estimates ranged from $1 trillion to $2 trillion, and CNBC reported investors were calling even $1.5 trillion "a stretch" amid AI-market jitters.

The huge net losses ($80B H1, $104B nine months) are mostly one-off, non-cash charges from changes in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities, not operating losses; comparing them across sources should be done carefully.

S-1 financials are being updated between the original Oct 26 filing (H1 2026 data), the Nov 2 amendment (Q3 data) and the Nov 10 amendment (price range); figures cited may be superseded by later amendments.

There is a discrepancy in secondary coverage: the Guardian calls the filing a "92-page document" (later describing 92 pages of risk), while CNBC describes an "over 300 page" S-1 with "more than 90 pages of risk factors" — the risk-factor section length (~90+ pages) is consistent across both.

passages.quote:
Today, Anthropic, PBC filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission relating to its proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock.

Anthropic intends to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.” The number of shares of Class A common stock to be offered and the price range for the proposed offering have not yet been determined.

The proposed offering consists of 825,000,000 shares of Class A common stock. Of these, 801,351,354 shares are being offered by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares are being offered by certain existing stockholders. Anthropic will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders. Anthropic also expects to grant the underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to an additional 123,750,000 shares of its Class A common stock.

The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.”

Anthropic said it will offer 825 million shares in its upcoming IPO at a price range between $70 and $78 per share, according to an [updated filing](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/2130357/000162828026072484/anthropicpbc-sx1ax2.htm) on Tuesday, bringing the 5-year-old artificial intelligence lab a step closer to a potentially historic Nasdaq debut.

The company is planning to price on Nov. 18 and trade on Nov. 19, according to people familiar with the details who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly. Anthropic is targeting retail allocation of about 20%, the people said, a much higher percentage than the typical initial public offering, which is 5% to 10% for retail investors.

For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Anthropic said it generated $33.24 billion in revenue up roughly 1,200% from the same period last year. It reported a $104 billion net loss during the nine-month period, though most of that was due to the change in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities. Anthropic lost $25.1 billion over the same stretch in 2025, the filing said.

Anthropic said in its amended filing Tuesday that its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.

In the amended S-1, Anthropic said it has entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure."

Anthropic said its compute and infrastructure expenses increased by $14.4 billion for the nine months ended Sept. 30, up 329% compared with the same period last year.

"As our compute and infrastructure capacity grows, the associated compute and infrastructure expenses have increased," Anthropic said in the filing.

Anthropic reported its cost of revenue as $2.38 billion in the first half of 2026, booking $16.29 billion in revenue during the same period and implying a gross margin of 85%.

Violeta Todorova, senior research analyst at Leverage Shares, told CNBC that the first-half revenue compared with just $1.16 billion in the first half of 2025, and asked whether it could grow to "keep pace with expectations."

"It is unclear how much it costs to generate each additional dollar of revenue as computing demand increases," she said.

But Anthropic's meteoric revenue growth slowed in the third quarter. It grew approximately 144% in the second quarter compared to the first quarter, followed by roughly 47% in the third quarter.

Anthropic's structure as a public benefit corporation [raises questions](https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/28/anthropic-pbc-what-its-structure-means-for-investors-.html), too. Seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, have special voting power through a single Class F share equal to 50.1% of total voting power over matters brought to a shareholder vote.

Anthropic describes its capital and corporate governance structure as having "no direct public company precedent," in the filing.

Here’s what you need to know: Anthropic is making a lot of money. It’s also losing a lot of it. The five-year-old firm has been valued between $1.5 and $2tn by some investors but did not list a target valuation in its S-1. Founded in 2021, the company has seen explosive growth every year of its existence.

    Anthropic brought in $16.3bn in revenue and lost $80bn in just the first half of 2026, though much of that was due to a $72.4bn one-off charge. In 2025, the company brought in $4.585bn and lost roughly $33.9bn, per the filing.

    [Column chart showing quarterly filings from Anthropic from Q1 2025 to Q2 2026. While revenues are increasing quarter over quarter, net losses are increasing at a faster rate.](https://interactive.guim.co.uk/datawrapper/embed/uOBkb/2/)

    Securing computing power accounts for the vast majority of Anthropic’s costs. The company spent nearly $9bn on AI infrastructure in the first half of this year, up from $2.3bn in the same period last year.

    Anthropic, unlike OpenAI, has made it clear that its customers are largely other businesses. “Frontier AI is most valuable in real-world settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest,” the company executives wrote in the filing.

    The company said its top five customers account for 25% of its business – which makes it risky business.

Anthropic’s most capable models are capable of providing “meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote in the filing.

    The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended”.

output.question: What are the key takeaways from Anthropic's S-1 filing?

key_facts.fact: Anthropic, PBC filed a registration statement on Form S-1 with the SEC for a proposed IPO of its Class A common stock, intending to list on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT"; share count and price range were not yet determined.
Anthropic had confidentially submitted a draft S-1 to the SEC on June 1, 2026, before the public filing.

In a Nov 10 amended filing Anthropic set the IPO at 825 million shares priced $70–$78 per share (801,351,354 offered by Anthropic, 23,648,646 by selling stockholders, plus a 30-day option on up to 123,750,000 more shares).

At the high end of the range Anthropic would net up to $64.35 billion in proceeds and could be worth up to $1.405 trillion fully diluted, up from the $965 billion valuation set in its May funding round; pricing was planned for Nov 18 and trading for Nov 19, with ~20% retail allocation targeted.

Amended S-1 reported $33.24 billion of revenue for the nine months ended Sept 30, 2026 (up ~1,200% year over year), a $104 billion net loss (mostly from changes in fair value of convertible notes and derivative liabilities; the same stretch of 2025 lost $25.1 billion), and Q3 revenue of roughly $17 billion (up ~1,127% year over year).
Anthropic said its run-rate revenue was roughly $81 billion at the end of October, up $10 billion from the previous month.

First-half 2026: revenue of $16.29 billion vs $1.16 billion in H1 2025, cost of revenue of $2.38 billion implying an 85% gross margin, with "substantially all" of cost of revenue tied to compute and infrastructure; quarterly growth decelerated from ~144% in Q2 to ~47% in Q3 (132% in Q1).
Anthropic lost about $80 billion in H1 2026 on $16.3 billion of revenue (much of it a $72.4 billion one-off charge); in 2025 it booked $4.585 billion of revenue and lost roughly $33.9 billion.

The amended S-1 disclosed purchase commitments and lease agreements of about $895.4 billion in aggregate committed spend, "substantially all of which is related to compute and infrastructure"; compute and infrastructure expenses rose $14.4 billion (up 329%) for the nine months ended Sept 30.

Governance: Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, and seven co-founders including CEO Dario Amodei hold special voting power via a single Class F share equal to 50.1% of total voting power; the filing calls its capital and governance structure as having "no direct public company precedent."

The filing contains more than 90 pages of risk factors and admits its AI safeguards "are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended"; it also cites an AI-orchestrated cyber-attack by a Chinese state-sponsored group targeting roughly 30 global targets.

Customer concentration: the top five customers account for 25% of Anthropic's business, and the business is largely enterprise/B2B ("deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest").

Anthropic spent nearly $9 billion on AI infrastructure in H1 2026, up from $2.3 billion in the same period a year earlier, and describes having historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand exceeded supply.

AMD, Broadcom, Google, Micron, Microsoft, Nvidia and TSMC agreed to purchase $26 billion of Anthropic Class N common stock in a private placement at the IPO price; the shares will not be registered in the offering and are not subject to underwriter lock-ups.
No target valuation was listed in the S-1; analyst estimates range between $1 trillion and $2 trillion, and CNBC reported that even $1.5 trillion was viewed by some investors as a "stretch."

The offering comes about five months after SpaceX's record IPO, and CNBC reports institutional demand is even stronger than SpaceX's at the same stage, with the book already covered at the $70–$78 range on an allocable basis.
